title: One who has compassion (Hebrews 4:14–16)
hook: a high priest tempted in all things like us, without sin
tomorrow: The substance of things hoped for

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word of God, sharper than a two-edged sword. Your line was living and effectual. Where did your verse land? Day six hundred one.

Before an operation, a nurse who once had the same surgery can say the same words as one who hasn't: it'll be okay. They land differently, because she's been there. Hebrews builds much of its argument around a picture from Israel's worship: the high priest, who once a year on the Day of Atonement entered the holiest place to seek mercy for the people. And today the preacher says something surprising about the high priest Christians have.
screen: `A NURSE WHO'S BEEN THERE.` → `THE HIGH PRIEST, ONCE A YEAR.` → `A HIGH PRIEST WHO UNDERSTANDS.`

segments.voice: First he says who it is: a great high priest who has passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, so hold fast to what you profess. Then the surprise: "For we have not a high priest, who can not have compassion on our infirmities: but one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The Greek verb for have compassion is sympathēsai: to suffer with, to feel alongside. Not pity from above. Fellow feeling from inside. Tempted in all things like as we are. Hebrews means it. A chapter later it says that in the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications with a strong cry and tears. The Gospels show him hungry in the desert, tempted there, exhausted, grieving at a friend's tomb, in anguish in Gethsemane. And yet without sin. Catholic teaching holds both together. The Council of Chalcedon said he is like us in all things but sin. Sinlessness, in this picture, doesn't make him distant from the tempted. Some Christian writers have argued that one who never gave way under temptation felt its full weight, and so knows its full strength. Then the invitation: "Let us go therefore with confidence to the throne of grace: that we may obtain mercy, and find grace in seasonable aid." With confidence. The Greek word means boldness, the freedom to speak openly. Seasonable aid means help at the right moment, when you need it. Catholics hear this invitation in many places: in personal prayer, before the tabernacle, and in confession, where they believe Christ's mercy meets them through the priest. He understands. That's the whole of today's line.
screen: `A GREAT HIGH PRIEST.` · `SYMPATHĒSAI: TO SUFFER WITH.` · `TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS, WITHOUT SIN.` · `GO WITH CONFIDENCE.` · then, large: `ONE TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS LIKE AS WE ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one weakness. Settle, and breathe. Think of one weakness, the kind you'd rather nobody saw. A temptation that keeps winning. A fear. A failure you keep repeating. Don't hide it, and don't beat yourself up about it either. Just hold it up, honestly. If you pray, you can bring it to Christ as Hebrews invites: with confidence, to someone who understands. If you don't, simply picture telling it to someone who has been exactly there, and notice what that feels like. The bell holds the time.
One who has compassion. Hebrews' picture of Jesus as high priest: tempted in all things like us, without sin, and able to suffer with us. Today's word.
Your line: he understands. Today, when you're hard on someone for a weakness, remember one you share, and speak to them as someone who's been there. Day six hundred one.

screen: `DAY 601 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS HOPED FOR.`

howItsDone: Catholics bring their weaknesses to Christ in personal prayer, in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, and in the sacrament of penance, where they believe Christ forgives through the priest.

original.note: Greek: to suffer with, to feel alongside (Hebrews 4:15).

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was too holy to know what temptation feels like.
what it means: our high priest was tempted in every way like us, without sin, and so he suffers with us.
what a scholar hears: sympathēsai; parrēsia, boldness; Hebrews 5:7's strong cry and tears; Chalcedon's 'like us in all things but sin'.

sources.ref: Council of Chalcedon (451); Catechism of the Catholic Church 467, 540

notes: Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) described respectfully as the background Hebrews draws on; no contrast that disparages Israel's worship. Confirm tone.
sympathēsai → sympathy; parrēsia ('confidence') as boldness/freedom of speech. Confirm.
Argument that sinlessness means feeling the full force of temptation: a common theological point (e.g. C. S. Lewis, Westcott), stated without attribution. Confirm acceptable.
CCC 467 quotes Chalcedon ('like us in all things but sin'). Confirm.

Review edit: the sinlessness-and-temptation argument is now attributed ('Some Christian writers have argued') rather than stated as fact; 'sweating in fear in Gethsemane' changed to 'in anguish in Gethsemane', since Luke 22:43–44 (the sweat like drops of blood) is textually uncertain and absent from some early manuscripts.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they feel; 'whole argument' softened to 'much of its argument'; cut the English 'sympathy' etymology (voice, screen, match, myth, original), which also repeated day 600's energy/critic move; 'many Christian writers' now 'some'; practice no longer assumes shame; Hebrews 9:7 added for 'once a year'.
